claim: The dinoflagellate genus Hematodinium is detrimental to crustaceans globally.
source: The dinoflagellate genus Hematodinium is detrimental to crustaceans globally – considered to suppress the innate defences of hosts, making them more susceptible to co-infections.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract supported by the broader literature context and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Hematodinium is considered to suppress the innate defences of hosts, making them more susceptible to co-infections.
source: The dinoflagellate genus Hematodinium is detrimental to crustaceans globally – considered to suppress the innate defences of hosts, making them more susceptible to co-infections.
evidence: This represents a prevailing hypothesis in the field that the authors are testing, referenced throughout the introduction.

claim: Evidence supporting immune suppression by Hematodinium is largely anecdotal and sourced from diffuse accounts of compromised decapods.
source: Evidence supporting immune suppression is largely anecdotal and sourced from diffuse accounts of compromised decapods.
evidence: This is an assessment of the existing literature presented in the abstract and supported by the introduction discussion.

claim: 1191 crabs were sampled across the year-long survey, with 603 from the Dock and 588 from the Pier.
source: Overall, 1191 crabs were sampled across the year-long survey, 603 from the Dock and 588 from the Pier (Davies et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the sample size with citation to the previous study.

claim: 13.6% of crabs were Hematodinium-positive via PCR alone.
source: Of these crabs, 13.6% were Hematodinium-positive via PCR alone, with 9.3% confirmed clinical infections using molecular and tissue diagnostics.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from PCR diagnostics performed on the crab population.

claim: 9.3% of crabs had confirmed clinical Hematodinium infections using molecular and tissue diagnostics.
source: Of these crabs, 13.6% were Hematodinium-positive via PCR alone, with 9.3% confirmed clinical infections using molecular and tissue diagnostics.
evidence: This is a quantitative result combining PCR and histological examination.

claim: 162 Hematodinium-positive crabs were size/sex-matched to 162 Hematodinium-free crabs out of 1191 analysed.
source: We identified 162 Hematodinium-positive crabs and size/sex-matched these to 162 Hematodinium-free crabs out of 1191 analysed.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and sample selection methodology.

claim: No significant differences in occurrence, severity, or composition of collateral infections were found between Hematodinium-positive and Hematodinium-free crabs at either site.
source: We found no significant differences in occurrence, severity, or composition of collateral infections between Hematodinium-positive and Hematodinium-free crabs at either site, but crucially, we recorded site-restricted blends of pathogens.
evidence: This is a primary finding from statistical analysis of co-infection data across both sites.

claim: Site-restricted blends of pathogens were recorded.
source: We found no significant differences in occurrence, severity, or composition of collateral infections between Hematodinium-positive and Hematodinium-free crabs at either site, but crucially, we recorded site-restricted blends of pathogens.
evidence: This is a finding from the comparative analysis of pathogen composition between the two study sites.

claim: No gross signs of host cell immune reactivity towards Hematodinium were found in the presence or absence of other pathogens.
source: We found no gross signs of host cell immune reactivity towards Hematodinium in the presence or absence of other pathogens.
evidence: This is based on histological and haematological observations of crab tissues and haemolymph.

claim: Hematodinium sp. is not the proximal driver of co-infections in shore crabs.
source: We contend Hematodinium sp. is not the proximal driver of co-infections in shore crabs, which suggests an evolutionary drive towards latency in this environmentally plastic host.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the collective data showing no association between Hematodinium presence and co-infections.

claim: There is an evolutionary drive towards latency of Hematodinium sp. in the environmentally plastic shore crab host.
source: We contend Hematodinium sp. is not the proximal driver of co-infections in shore crabs, which suggests an evolutionary drive towards latency in this environmentally plastic host.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings suggesting an evolutionary strategy, based on the lack of immune response and co-infection patterns.

claim: Dinoflagellates of the genus Hematodinium include at least three parasitic species: H. perezi, H. australis, and Hematodinium sp.
source: Dinoflagellates of the genus Hematodinium include at least three parasitic species, H. perezi, H. australis, and Hematodinium sp., which target a myriad of crustacean hosts, as far south as Australia (Gornik et al., 2013) and as far north as Greenland (Eigemann et al., 2010).
evidence: This is taxonomic information supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Hematodinium species target crustacean hosts as far south as Australia and as far north as Greenland.
source: Dinoflagellates of the genus Hematodinium include at least three parasitic species, H. perezi, H. australis, and Hematodinium sp., which target a myriad of crustacean hosts, as far south as Australia (Gornik et al., 2013) and as far north as Greenland (Eigemann et al., 2010).
evidence: This describes the geographic distribution of Hematodinium species with specific citations.

claim: Epizootics of Hematodinium spp. can devastate localised communities, fishery and aquaculture industries.
source: Epizootics of Hematodinium spp. can devastate localised communities, fishery and aquaculture industries with langoustines, shrimp, and blue crabs representing some of the >40 known susceptible marine beasties (Albalat et al., 2016; Albalat et al., 2012; Davies et al., 2019a; Li et al., 2013; Messick and Shields, 2000; Rowley et al., 2015; Shields et al., 2003; Small, 2012; Small et al., 2012; Small et al., 2006; Smith et al., 2015; Stentiford et al., 2001; Stentiford and Shields, 2005; Wilhelm and Mialhe, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations documenting the impact of Hematodinium on various crustacean populations.

claim: More than 40 marine crustacean species are known to be susceptible to Hematodinium spp., including langoustines, shrimp, and blue crabs.
source: Epizootics of Hematodinium spp. can devastate localised communities, fishery and aquaculture industries with langoustines, shrimp, and blue crabs representing some of the >40 known susceptible marine beasties (Albalat et al., 2016; Albalat et al., 2012; Davies et al., 2019a; Li et al., 2013; Messick and Shields, 2000; Rowley et al., 2015; Shields et al., 2003; Small, 2012; Small et al., 2012; Small et al., 2006; Smith et al., 2015; Stentiford et al., 2001; Stentiford and Shields, 2005; Wilhelm and Mialhe, 1996).
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about host range supported by extensive citations.

claim: Signs of Hematodinium infection include carapace and blood (haemolymph) discolouration from aggressive proliferation of parasite morphotypes.
source: Signs of infection include carapace and blood (haemolymph) discolouration from the aggressive proliferation of parasite morphotypes within the liquid and solid (hepatopancreas) tissues, and lethargy caused by metabolic exhaustion (e.g., hypoproteinaemia).
evidence: This describes clinical signs of infection based on established knowledge and observations.

claim: Hematodinium infection causes lethargy in crustacean hosts due to metabolic exhaustion such as hypoproteinaemia.
source: Signs of infection include carapace and blood (haemolymph) discolouration from the aggressive proliferation of parasite morphotypes within the liquid and solid (hepatopancreas) tissues, and lethargy caused by metabolic exhaustion (e.g., hypoproteinaemia).
evidence: This describes a pathological consequence of infection supported by the literature.

claim: Advanced colonisation of the haemolymph by Hematodinium leads to a severe decline in circulating immune cells (total haemocyte counts).
source: The advanced colonisation of the haemolymph leads to a severe decline in the number of circulating immune cells (i.e., total haemocyte counts) and regional tissue necrosis (e.g., muscle) – conditions that are likely to be fatal (Rowley et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes a pathological effect of infection with citation support.

claim: Advanced Hematodinium infection causes regional tissue necrosis in muscle tissue.
source: The advanced colonisation of the haemolymph leads to a severe decline in the number of circulating immune cells (i.e., total haemocyte counts) and regional tissue necrosis (e.g., muscle) – conditions that are likely to be fatal (Rowley et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes pathological changes observed in infected crustaceans with citation.

claim: Advanced Hematodinium infection conditions are likely to be fatal to the host.
source: The advanced colonisation of the haemolymph leads to a severe decline in the number of circulating immune cells (i.e., total haemocyte counts) and regional tissue necrosis (e.g., muscle) – conditions that are likely to be fatal (Rowley et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference about disease outcome based on the severity of pathological changes and citation.

claim: There is little direct evidence supporting the view that Hematodinium spp. suppress crustacean immune defences.
source: Little direct evidence supports the reported view that Hematodinium spp. suppress the crustacean immune defences, thereby enabling the parasite to despoil its host of resources.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of the existing literature on Hematodinium immunosuppression.

claim: Direct suppression of host defences by Hematodinium would leave the host vulnerable to other infectious or opportunistic agents.
source: Furthermore, direct suppression of the host's defences would leave it vulnerable to other infectious or opportunistic agents, leading to micro-scale competition with the dinoflagellate.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the consequences of immunosuppression.

claim: Co-infections of Hematodinium-positive tanner crabs (Chionoecetes bairdi) with bacterial septicaemia and ciliates have been characterized.
source: Several studies have characterised so-called co-infections of Hematodinium-positive crustaceans, including bacterial septicaemia and ciliates in tanner crabs (Chionoecetes bairdi; Love et al., 1993; Meyers et al., 1987), and yeast-like mycosis in edible (Cancer pagurus; Smith et al., 2013) and velvet swimming crabs (Necora puber; Stentiford et al., 2003).
evidence: This summarizes findings from cited studies on co-infections.

claim: Co-infections of Hematodinium-positive edible crabs (Cancer pagurus) and velvet swimming crabs (Necora puber) with yeast-like mycosis have been characterized.
source: Several studies have characterised so-called co-infections of Hematodinium-positive crustaceans, including bacterial septicaemia and ciliates in tanner crabs (Chionoecetes bairdi; Love et al., 1993; Meyers et al., 1987), and yeast-like mycosis in edible (Cancer pagurus; Smith et al., 2013) and velvet swimming crabs (Necora puber; Stentiford et al., 2003).
evidence: This summarizes findings from cited studies on co-infections.

claim: Co-infections in Hematodinium-positive crabs elicit an immune response including haemocyte-directed nodulation and melanisation events.
source: These co-infections elicit an immune response – leading to haemocyte-directed nodulation and melanisation events (revealed by haematology and histopathology) – but during events, Hematodinium are not targeted.
evidence: This describes observed immune responses to co-infections based on histological evidence.

claim: During immune responses to co-infections, Hematodinium parasites are not targeted by the host immune system.
source: These co-infections elicit an immune response – leading to haemocyte-directed nodulation and melanisation events (revealed by haematology and histopathology) – but during events, Hematodinium are not targeted.
evidence: This is an observation from histopathological studies suggesting immune evasion.

claim: The lack of immune targeting of Hematodinium suggests an immune-evasion strategy at the cellular level rather than immune suppression.
source: Such observations suggest an immune-evasion strategy at least at the cellular level, rather than immune suppression.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observation that Hematodinium is not targeted during immune responses to other pathogens.

claim: Li et al. (2019, 2015a, 2015b) presented evidence for immune activation of the Japanese blue crab (Portunus trituberculatus) containing H. perezi based on measurements of immune gene levels (mRNAs), differential protein expression in the hepatopancreas, and some enzymatic activities.
source: Conversely, Li et al., 2019; Li et al., 2015a; Li et al., 2015b presented evidence for immune activation of the Japanese blue crab (Portunus trituberculatus) containing H. perezi based on measurements of immune gene levels (mRNAs), differential protein expression in the hepatopancreas, and some enzymatic activities (e.g., phenoloxidase).
evidence: This summarizes findings from cited studies showing immune activation.

claim: No Hematodinium-derived effectors were identified in studies of Japanese blue crab immune responses.
source: These data are valuable as there are few studies on the interaction between Hematodinium spp. and crustacean innate immunity; however, no Hematodinium-derived effectors were identified.
evidence: This is a critical observation about the limitations of previous studies.

claim: Co-infection is commonly observed in both terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems.
source: Co-infection, whereby a single individual or species is host to multiple infections (microbes or micro/macro-parasites) is commonly observed in both terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems.
evidence: This is a general statement about co-infection patterns based on ecological knowledge.

claim: In open-water fisheries and aquaculture, co-infections may be more prevalent due to a large variety of environmental reservoirs and high densities, respectively.
source: In open-water fisheries and aquaculture, co-infections may be more prevalent due to a large variety of environmental reservoirs and high densities, respectively.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about factors influencing co-infection prevalence in different environments.

claim: Shore crabs (Carcinus maenas) are potential reservoirs of disease, notably Hematodinium spp.
source: Recently, we investigated the potential role of non-commercial, common shore crabs (Carcinus maenas) as potential reservoirs of disease, notably Hematodinium spp. (Davies et al., 2019a), as they are co-located with many high-value shellfish, for example, edible crabs.
evidence: This describes a previous investigation with citation.

claim: Shore crabs are co-located with many high-value shellfish such as edible crabs.
source: Recently, we investigated the potential role of non-commercial, common shore crabs (Carcinus maenas) as potential reservoirs of disease, notably Hematodinium spp. (Davies et al., 2019a), as they are co-located with many high-value shellfish, for example, edible crabs.
evidence: This is an ecological observation about the spatial distribution of crab species.

claim: The parasitic barnacle Sacculina carcini was noted during the initial survey of shore crabs.
source: During our initial survey, we noted the presence of several disease conditions in addition to that caused by Hematodinium sp., such as the parasitic barnacle Sacculina carcini (Rowley et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an observation from the survey with citation.

claim: 93 crabs were used to assess nucleotide diversity of the mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase I subunit (COI) gene (48 from Pier, 45 from Dock).
source: To establish whether crabs at either site represented distinct populations, we assessed the nucleotide diversity of the mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase I subunit (COI) gene from 93 crabs collected for the February 2018 screen (n = 48/Pier; n = 45/Dock) using a 588 bp fragment as recommended by Roman, 2004.
evidence: This describes the sample size and methodology for population genetic analysis.

claim: Crabs from the Dock location yielded 18 COI haplotypes.
source: Crabs sampled from the Dock and Pier locations yielded 18 and 19 haplotypes, respectively (GenBank accession numbers MT547783-MT547812).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from genetic analysis with GenBank accession numbers provided.

claim: Crabs from the Pier location yielded 19 COI haplotypes.
source: Crabs sampled from the Dock and Pier locations yielded 18 and 19 haplotypes, respectively (GenBank accession numbers MT547783-MT547812).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from genetic analysis with GenBank accession numbers provided.

claim: 72 COI haplotypes were identified among 320 individual nucleotide sequences of C. maenas.
source: In total, 72 COI haplotypes were identified among the 320 individual nucleotide sequences (481 bp in length) of C. maenas (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from genetic analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Eight haplotypes observed in the Dock location were unique to this site (private haplotypes).
source: Eight haplotypes observed in the Dock location were unique to this site (i.e., private haplotypes), and 10 private haplotypes were observed in the Pier location.
evidence: This is a result from genetic diversity analysis.

claim: Ten private haplotypes were observed in the Pier location.
source: Eight haplotypes observed in the Dock location were unique to this site (i.e., private haplotypes), and 10 private haplotypes were observed in the Pier location.
evidence: This is a result from genetic diversity analysis.

claim: Seven haplotypes were shared between the Dock and Pier locations.
source: Seven haplotypes were shared between the Dock and Pier locations.
evidence: This is a result from genetic diversity analysis indicating gene flow or common ancestry.

claim: The most common C. maenas haplotype globally (haplotype h1) was also the most common haplotype in both the Dock (frequency 0.33) and Pier (frequency 0.31) locations.
source: Globally, the most common C. maenas haplotype (i.e., haplotype h1 shown in yellow in Figure 1) was also the most common haplotype observed in the Dock (frequency of 0.33) and Pier (frequency of 0.31) locations.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from haplotype frequency analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Similar genetic diversity was observed between the Dock and Pier locations.
source: A similar genetic diversity (i.e., number of haplotypes, Hd and π) was observed between the Dock and Pier locations (Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: This is a conclusion from genetic diversity metrics presented in the appendix table.

claim: Significant pairwise genetic differentiation (Fst estimates between 0.604 and 0.902) was observed between European off-shelf locations and all western/northern locations.
source: Significant pairwise genetic differentiation (Fst estimates between 0.604 and 0.902) was observed between European off-shelf locations (located in Iceland and Faroe Islands) and all western/northern locations (Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: This is a result from population genetic analysis showing geographic structure.

claim: No significant Fst value was observed between the Dock and Pier locations, indicating that crabs from the two sites were genetically similar.
source: No significant Fst value was observed between the Dock and Pier locations, indicating that the crabs from the two sites were genetically similar (Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: This is a statistical result indicating lack of genetic differentiation between the two study sites.

claim: No genetic differentiation was observed between Hematodinium parasites from the two locations (Fst = 0.004, p=0.161).
source: No genetic differentiation (Fst = 0.004, p=0.161) was observed between the two locations.
evidence: This is a statistical result from genetic analysis of Hematodinium ITS-1 sequences.

claim: 70 ITS-1 haplotypes were identified among 102 individual nucleotide sequences of Hematodinium sp.
source: 70 ITS-1 haplotypes were identified among the 102 individual nucleotide sequences (218–229 bp in length) of Hematodinium sp. (Appendix 1—table 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from genetic analysis of the parasite.

claim: 31 Hematodinium haplotypes were observed in the Pier location and 41 in the Dock location.
source: In total, 31 and 41 haplotypes were observed in the Pier and Dock locations, respectively (Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from genetic analysis of Hematodinium.

claim: Only two Hematodinium haplotypes were shared between the Pier and Dock locations.
source: Only two haplotypes were shared between the two locations, and the most common haplotype was present at a frequency of 0.29 in the Pier and 0.23 in the Dock.
evidence: This is a result showing limited haplotype sharing between sites for the parasite.

claim: High genetic diversity was observed in Hematodinium from both locations with nucleotide diversity of 0.0130 in the Pier and 0.0274 in the Dock.
source: A high genetic diversity was observed in both locations with a nucleotide diversity of 0.0130 and 0.0274 in the Pier and Dock, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from genetic diversity analysis of the parasite.

claim: 24.7% (40/162) of Hematodinium-positive crabs had one or more co-infections across both locations.
source: Across both locations, 24.7% (40/162) of Hematodinium-positive crabs had one or more co-infections (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from disease screening shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: 23.5% (38/162) of Hematodinium-free crabs had one or more infection.
source: In terms of Hematodinium-free crabs, 23.5% (38/162) had one or more infection.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from disease screening of control crabs.

claim: In the Dock location, 27.6% (24/87) of Hematodinium-positive crabs were co-infected.
source: In the Dock and Pier locations, 27.6% (24/87) and 21.3% (16/75) of Hematodinium-positive crabs were co-infected, with 20.7% (18/87) and 26.7% (20/75) of the Hematodinium-free crabs, respectively, testing positive for these notable diseases (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from disease screening at the Dock site shown in Figure 2.

claim: In the Pier location, 21.3% (16/75) of Hematodinium-positive crabs were co-infected.
source: In the Dock and Pier locations, 27.6% (24/87) and 21.3% (16/75) of Hematodinium-positive crabs were co-infected, with 20.7% (18/87) and 26.7% (20/75) of the Hematodinium-free crabs, respectively, testing positive for these notable diseases (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from disease screening at the Pier site shown in Figure 2.

claim: In the Dock location, 20.7% (18/87) of Hematodinium-free crabs tested positive for diseases.
source: In the Dock and Pier locations, 27.6% (24/87) and 21.3% (16/75) of Hematodinium-positive crabs were co-infected, with 20.7% (18/87) and 26.7% (20/75) of the Hematodinium-free crabs, respectively, testing positive for these notable diseases (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from disease screening of control crabs at the Dock site.

claim: In the Pier location, 26.7% (20/75) of Hematodinium-free crabs tested positive for diseases.
source: In the Dock and Pier locations, 27.6% (24/87) and 21.3% (16/75) of Hematodinium-positive crabs were co-infected, with 20.7% (18/87) and 26.7% (20/75) of the Hematodinium-free crabs, respectively, testing positive for these notable diseases (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from disease screening of control crabs at the Pier site.

claim: There were no significant differences between the number of disease agents between Hematodinium-positive and Hematodinium-free crabs, regardless of location (p=0.8967 overall, p=0.3759 Dock, p=0.5667 Pier).
source: There were no significant differences between the number of disease agents between Hematodinium-positive and Hematodinium-free crabs, regardless of location (p=0.8967 overall, p=0.3759 Dock, p=0.5667 Pier, Fisher's exact test, two-sided, Figure 2a–c).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Fisher's exact test comparing co-infection rates.

claim: In the Dock location, three out of eight co-infections were observed in crabs: Vibrio spp., microsporidians, and S. carcini.
source: In the Dock location, three out of eight co-infections were observed in crabs (Vibrio spp., microsporidians, and S. carcini, Figure 2e, Figure 3); and in the Pier location, four out of eight co-infections were observed (Vibrio spp., Haplosporidium sp., trematode parasites, and fungal species, Figure 2f, Figure 3).
evidence: This is a result from pathogen screening showing site-specific disease profiles.

claim: In the Pier location, four out of eight co-infections were observed in crabs: Vibrio spp., Haplosporidium sp., trematode parasites, and fungal species.
source: In the Dock location, three out of eight co-infections were observed in crabs (Vibrio spp., microsporidians, and S. carcini, Figure 2e, Figure 3); and in the Pier location, four out of eight co-infections were observed (Vibrio spp., Haplosporidium sp., trematode parasites, and fungal species, Figure 2f, Figure 3).
evidence: This is a result from pathogen screening showing site-specific disease profiles.

claim: The Hematodinium load quantified from haemolymph correlated positively (p<0.0001) with the severity of infection in the gill and hepatopancreas.
source: Overall, the Hematodinium load quantified from the liquid tissue using haemocytometry – number of parasites per mL haemolymph – correlated positively (p<0.0001) with the severity of infection in the gill and hepatopancreas graded 0–4 from histopathology (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a statistical result showing correlation between parasite load in different tissues.

claim: No co-infection revealed a significant relationship with Hematodinium sp. in the dataset overall or when separated by site.
source: Models were run using Hematodinium sp. as the response variable to determine any associations between Hematodinium presence and co-infections (Sacculina, trematodes, haplosporidians, microsporidians, Vibrio spp., and fungal species); however, no co-infection revealed a significant relationship with Hematodinium sp. in the dataset overall, nor when separated by site (Supplementary file 2—table 1, models S4–S6; Supplementary file 2—table 2, models S7–S11).
evidence: This is a result from binomial logistic regression models testing associations.

claim: The number of bacterial CFUs was significantly higher in the haemolymph of Hematodinium-affected crabs compared to Hematodinium-free crabs in the Dock location only (Mann–Whitney U = 2899, p=0.0276).
source: The number of bacterial CFUs was significantly higher in the haemolymph of Hematodinium-affected crabs compared to Hematodinium-free crabs, and in the Dock location only (Figure 3g; Mann–Whitney U = 2899, p=0.0276 two-tailed).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Mann-Whitney test comparing bacterial loads, shown in Figure 3g.

claim: Size (carapace width) was associated with the presence of one or more co-infections.
source: Model 1, the reduced model, revealed that size (carapace width [CW]) was associated with the presence of one or more co-infections (Table 1, model 1).
evidence: This is a result from binomial logistic regression analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: Smaller crabs were significantly more likely to display co-infections compared to those that were disease-free (p=0.0137, mean ± SEM: 46.26 ± 1.16 vs. 49.80 ± 0.67 mm).
source: Smaller crabs were significantly more likely to display co-infections compared to those that were 'disease-free' (p=0.0137, mean ± SEM: 46.26 ± 1.16 vs. 49.80 ± 0.67 mm, respectively; Figure 4a).
evidence: This is a statistical result from regression analysis with quantitative data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Hematodinium presence, location, season, sex, crab colour, fouling, limb loss, and bacterial CFU number did not have a significant effect on co-infection presence in the overall model.
source: Hematodinium presence, location, season, sex, crab colour, fouling (presence of epibionts), limb loss, and bacterial CFU number did not have a significant effect (Figure 4e and i; Supplementary file 2—table 1, model S1).
evidence: This is a result from binomial logistic regression showing non-significant variables.

claim: In Hematodinium-positive crabs, size (CW), crab colour, and limb loss are all associated with the presence of one or more co-infections.
source: Model 2, the reduced model using only Hematodinium-positive crabs and the presence of one or more co-infections as the response variable, revealed that size (CW), crab colour, and limb loss are all associated with the presence of one or more co-infections in the crabs (Table 1, model 2).
evidence: This is a result from binomial logistic regression analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: In Hematodinium-positive crabs, smaller crabs were significantly more likely to display co-infections (p=0.0392, mean ± SEM: 46.20 ± 1.66 vs. 49.93 ± 0.96 mm).
source: Smaller crabs were significantly more likely to display co-infections (p=0.0392, mean ± SEM: 46.20 ± 1.66 vs. 49.93 ± 0.96 mm, respectively; Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a statistical result from regression analysis shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Orange crabs were significantly less likely than green or yellow crabs to display co-infections (p=0.0404).
source: Orange crabs were significantly less likely than green or yellow crabs to display co-infections (p=0.0404; Figure 4f), and those crabs which suffered the loss of one or more limbs were 2.4-fold less likely to present a co-infection than those which had not lost limbs (p=0.0174, 11.9 vs. 28.57%, respectively; Figure 4j).
evidence: This is a statistical result from regression analysis shown in Figure 4f.

claim: Crabs which suffered the loss of one or more limbs were 2.4-fold less likely to present a co-infection than those which had not lost limbs (p=0.0174, 11.9 vs. 28.57%).
source: Orange crabs were significantly less likely than green or yellow crabs to display co-infections (p=0.0404; Figure 4f), and those crabs which suffered the loss of one or more limbs were 2.4-fold less likely to present a co-infection than those which had not lost limbs (p=0.0174, 11.9 vs. 28.57%, respectively; Figure 4j).
evidence: This is a statistical result from regression analysis shown in Figure 4j.

claim: In Hematodinium-positive crabs, location, season, sex, fouling, and bacterial CFU number did not have a significant effect on the presence of co-infections.
source: Location, season, sex, fouling (presence of epibionts), and bacterial CFU number did not have a significant effect on the presence of co-infections in Hematodinium-positive crabs (Supplementary file 2—table 1, model S2).
evidence: This is a result from binomial logistic regression showing non-significant variables.

claim: In Hematodinium-free control crabs, location, season, size (CW), sex, crab colour, fouling, limb loss, and CFU did not have any discernible effect on co-infection presence.
source: Using only control (Hematodinium-free) crabs and the presence of a 'co-infection' as the response variable produced no reduced model as the input variables, location, season, size (CW), sex, crab colour, fouling (presence of epibionts), limb loss, and CFU did not have any discernible effect (Figure 4c, g and k; Supplementary file 2—table 1, model S3).
evidence: This is a result from binomial logistic regression showing no significant predictors in control crabs.

claim: Limb loss was the single variable associated significantly with co-infection detection in crabs with clinical levels of Hematodinium sp.
source: Re-running models but restricting the crabs to those with clinical infections (n = 111) – that is, removing those that tested positive for Hematodinium sp. via PCR alone (n = 51) – did not yield any contradictory outcomes to those described above. Limb loss was the single variable associated significantly with co-infection detection in crabs with clinical levels of Hematodinium sp. (Figure 4d, h and l).
evidence: This is a result from regression analysis restricted to clinically infected crabs.

claim: The intensity of Hematodinium sp. infection (number of parasites per mL haemolymph) did not contribute significantly to the occurrence of one or more co-infection in crabs overall (p=0.335) or at either site (Pier, p=0.332, and Dock, p=0.822).
source: Crucially, additional models looking at the intensity of Hematodinium sp. infection (no. parasites per mL haemolymph) rather than simply yes/no did not contribute significantly to the occurrence of one or more co-infection in crabs overall (p=0.335) or at either site (Pier, p=0.332, and Dock, p=0.822; Supplementary file 2—table 2, models S12–S14).
evidence: This is a statistical result from regression models testing parasite load as a predictor.

claim: There was no apparent significant effect of Hematodinium sp. presence (F = 0.6453, p=0.533) on co-infection number.
source: There was no apparent significant effect of Hematodinium sp. presence (F = 0.6453, p=0.533) on co-infection number, but a significant effect of location (F = 94.281, p=0.001) on community structure.
evidence: This is a statistical result from multivariate analysis of co-infection community composition.

claim: There was a significant effect of location (F = 94.281, p=0.001) on co-infection community structure.
source: There was no apparent significant effect of Hematodinium sp. presence (F = 0.6453, p=0.533) on co-infection number, but a significant effect of location (F = 94.281, p=0.001) on community structure.
evidence: This is a statistical result from multivariate analysis showing location as a key determinant.

claim: The nMDS 2D ordination plots showed great overlap in the parasite community composition of Hematodinium-infected and Hematodinium-free crabs.
source: The non-metric multidimensional (nMDS) 2D ordination plots showed great overlap in the parasite community composition of Hematodinium-infected and Hematodinium-free crabs (Figure 5a) but varied greatly according to Dock and Pier locations (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is a result from nMDS ordination analysis shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The parasite community composition varied greatly according to Dock and Pier locations.
source: The non-metric multidimensional (nMDS) 2D ordination plots showed great overlap in the parasite community composition of Hematodinium-infected and Hematodinium-free crabs (Figure 5a) but varied greatly according to Dock and Pier locations (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is a result from nMDS ordination analysis shown in Figure 5b.

claim: PERMANOVA comparing co-infection community composition between Hematodinium-infected and control crabs yielded R2 = 0.00914 (approximately 0.1% of variation explained, p=0.482).
source: Permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) comparing the co-infection community composition between Hematodinium (via haemolymph quantitation)-infected and control (Hematodinium free) crabs yielded R2 = 0.00914, therefore ~0.1% of the variation in distances is explained by the grouping of controls vs. Hematodinium (p=0.482; Supplementary file 3) in contrast to location yielding R2 = 0.53818 (or nearly 54% of the variation in distances is explained by the grouping of Docks vs. Pier, p=0.001; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a statistical result from PERMANOVA showing minimal effect of Hematodinium status.

claim: PERMANOVA comparing co-infection community composition by location yielded R2 = 0.53818 (nearly 54% of variation explained, p=0.001).
source: Permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) comparing the co-infection community composition between Hematodinium (via haemolymph quantitation)-infected and control (Hematodinium free) crabs yielded R2 = 0.00914, therefore ~0.1% of the variation in distances is explained by the grouping of controls vs. Hematodinium (p=0.482; Supplementary file 3) in contrast to location yielding R2 = 0.53818 (or nearly 54% of the variation in distances is explained by the grouping of Docks vs. Pier, p=0.001; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a statistical result from PERMANOVA showing strong effect of location.

claim: Whether or not a crab had a subclinical or progressive Hematodinium sp. infection did not make a difference in the composition of associated/collateral pathogens.
source: Therefore, whether or not a crab had a subclinical or progressive Hematodinium sp. infection did not make a difference in the composition of associated/collateral pathogens.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the PERMANOVA and nMDS analyses.

claim: Co-infection community structure was determined by location, differing between the Dock and Pier.
source: Rather, co-infection community structure was determined by location, differing between the Dock and Pier.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the multivariate analyses showing location as the primary determinant.

claim: The differences between Dock and Pier locations were mostly driven by the presence of Sacculina, which was found exclusively in the Docks.
source: The differences between Dock and Pier locations were mostly driven by the presence of Sacculina, this being found exclusively in the Docks, as well as trematode parasites, haplosporidians, and fungal species, all of which were more abundant in the Pier location.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the multivariate analysis results identifying key drivers of site differences.

claim: Trematode parasites, haplosporidians, and fungal species were more abundant in the Pier location.
source: The differences between Dock and Pier locations were mostly driven by the presence of Sacculina, this being found exclusively in the Docks, as well as trematode parasites, haplosporidians, and fungal species, all of which were more abundant in the Pier location.
evidence: This is a result from comparative analysis of pathogen abundance between sites.

claim: Temperature measurements during the year-long survey were similar between the Pier and Dock locations (paired t-test, p=0.5329), 13.3°C ± 1.5°C and 13.6°C ± 1.6°C, respectively.
source: Temperature measurements recorded during the year-long disease survey were similar between the Pier and Dock locations (paired t-test, wo-sided; p=0.5329), 13.3°C ± 1.5°C and 13.6°C ± 1.6°C, respectively.
evidence: This is a result from environmental monitoring with statistical comparison.

claim: Differences in salinity levels between the Pier (30.5 ± 0.9 PSU) and Dock (28.9 ± 0.6 PSU) were subtle but statistically significant (Wilcoxon, p=0.0425).
source: Differences in salinity levels between the Pier (30.5 ± 0.9 PSU) and Dock (28.9 ± 0.6 PSU) were subtle but statistically significant (Wilcoxon, matched pairs; p=0.0425).
evidence: This is a result from environmental monitoring with statistical comparison.

claim: No evidence of crab haemocyte reactivity towards Hematodinium sp. was found in the absence or presence of other disease-causing agents (n = 162).
source: We found no evidence of crab haemocyte reactivity towards Hematodinium sp. in the absence or presence of other disease-causing agents (n = 162; Figure 6) either by observing haemolymph freshly withdrawn from the haemocoel using phase contrast microscopy (Figure 6a) or tissue histopathology (e.g., gills and hepatopancreas).
evidence: This is a result from microscopic and histological examination shown in Figure 6.

claim: Crab haemocytes recognised and responded to other pathogens and damaged host tissues, regardless of Hematodinium sp. presence.
source: Ostensibly, crab haemocytes recognised and responded to other pathogens (Figure 6b) and damaged host tissues (Figure 6c), regardless of Hematodinium sp. presence.
evidence: This is an observation from histological examination shown in Figure 6b and 6c.

claim: Even when haemocytes infiltrated tissues in large numbers, the resident Hematodinium sp. were not caught up in the ensheathment process.
source: In fact, even when haemocytes infiltrated tissues in large numbers, the resident Hematodinium sp. were not caught up in the ensheathment process (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is an observation from histological examination shown in Figure 6d.

claim: In vitro phagocytosis assays using Hematodinium sp. and haemocytes from disease-free crabs (n = 6) showed no gross or discernible signs of haemocyte-driven phagocytosis, degranulation, or capsule/nodule formation over the 2 hr period.
source: Additionally, we performed in vitro phagocytosis assays using Hematodinium sp. isolated from a heavily infected donor crab and haemocytes from apparent disease-free crabs (n = 6). There were no gross or discernible signs of haemocyte-driven phagocytosis, degranulation, or capsule/nodule formation over the 2 hr period.
evidence: This is a result from in vitro experimental assays.

claim: Hematodinium spp. outbreaks can wreak havoc on blue crab populations in the USA.
source: Hematodinium spp. outbreaks can wreak havoc on blue crab populations in the USA (Messick, 1994; Messick and Shields, 2000; Shields et al., 2003), cultured decapods in China (Huang et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021; Coates and Rowley, 2022), and represent a persistent scourge on langoustine fisheries in Scotland (Albalat et al., 2016; Albalat et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations documenting impacts on blue crab populations.

claim: Hematodinium spp. represent a persistent scourge on langoustine fisheries in Scotland.
source: Hematodinium spp. outbreaks can wreak havoc on blue crab populations in the USA (Messick, 1994; Messick and Shields, 2000; Shields et al., 2003), cultured decapods in China (Huang et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021; Coates and Rowley, 2022), and represent a persistent scourge on langoustine fisheries in Scotland (Albalat et al., 2016; Albalat et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations documenting impacts on langoustine fisheries.

claim: The infectivity and pathobiology of Hematodinium spp. in commercial hosts are well characterised.
source: Although the infectivity and pathobiology of Hematodinium spp. in these hosts are well characterised (Small et al., 2006), outside of commercial settings, their role(s) as ecological regulators of crustacean populations are largely overlooked.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge with citation support.

claim: Outside of commercial settings, the roles of Hematodinium spp. as ecological regulators of crustacean populations are largely overlooked.
source: Although the infectivity and pathobiology of Hematodinium spp. in these hosts are well characterised (Small et al., 2006), outside of commercial settings, their role(s) as ecological regulators of crustacean populations are largely overlooked.
evidence: This is an assessment of the research gap in the field.

claim: Davies et al., 2019a recognised a 13.6% prevalence of Hematodinium sp. among shore crabs using targeted PCR.
source: Davies et al., 2019a recognised a 13.6% prevalence of Hematodinium sp. among these crabs using targeted PCR and reported that no significant differences in the spatial or temporal profiles of the disease between the two sites existed.
evidence: This cites a specific finding from a previous study by the authors.

claim: No significant differences in the spatial or temporal profiles of Hematodinium disease between the two sites existed.
source: Davies et al., 2019a recognised a 13.6% prevalence of Hematodinium sp. among these crabs using targeted PCR and reported that no significant differences in the spatial or temporal profiles of the disease between the two sites existed.
evidence: This cites a finding from a previous study by the authors.

claim: Six out of eight alternative diseases were identified in the host: four via both molecular and histopathology screening, and two via histopathology alone.
source: In the host, we identified six out of the eight alternative diseases – four via both molecular and histopathology screening, and a further two via the latter technique.
evidence: This summarizes the disease detection results using different diagnostic methods.

claim: Data from crabs and eDNA attributed the variation in collateral infection composition to location, and not to the presence of Hematodinium sp.
source: Data from crabs and eDNA attributed the variation in collateral infection composition to location, and not to the presence of Hematodinium sp.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the combined analysis of crab and environmental DNA data.

claim: Hematodinium-positive crabs from the Dock contained significantly higher levels of cultivable bacterial CFUs in the haemolymph when compared to Hematodinium-free animals, but this was not the case at the Pier or when both sites were combined.
source: For example, Hematodinium-positive crabs from the Dock contained significantly higher levels of cultivable bacterial CFUs in the haemolymph when compared to Hematodinium-free animals, but this was not the case at the Pier, or when both sites were combined (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a result from bacterial culture analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The parasitic castrator S. carcini was found exclusively in the Dock site.
source: The parasitic castrator, S. carcini, was found exclusively in the Dock site and those crabs specifically contained very high levels of CFUs, which we determined previously to be pathognomonic of S. carcini infection (and not Hematodinium sp.) in this species (Rowley et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a result from pathogen screening showing site-specific distribution.

claim: Crabs infected with S. carcini contained very high levels of CFUs, which is pathognomonic of S. carcini infection (and not Hematodinium sp.) in this species.
source: The parasitic castrator, S. carcini, was found exclusively in the Dock site and those crabs specifically contained very high levels of CFUs, which we determined previously to be pathognomonic of S. carcini infection (and not Hematodinium sp.) in this species (Rowley et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from bacterial culture analysis with citation to previous work.

claim: Binomial logistic regression models revealed CW (small size), and not season or sex, as a significant predictor variable of co-infections overall.
source: Herein, binomial logistic regression models revealed CW (small), and not season or sex, as a significant predictor variable of co-infections overall.
evidence: This is a result from statistical modeling.

claim: In a previous study, seasonality and sex, but not size, were determined as the overall key predictor variables of Hematodinium sp. in crabs.
source: This contrasts with our previous study (Davies et al., 2019a) in which we determined seasonality and sex, but not size, as the overall key predictor variables of Hematodinium sp. in crabs.
evidence: This cites findings from a previous study for comparison.

claim: If Hematodinium was a determinant for co-infections, a seasonal pattern or sex bias should be observed, but neither is present.
source: If Hematodinium was a determinant for co-infections, we should see a seasonal pattern, or sex bias, but we do not.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the absence of expected patterns if Hematodinium caused co-infections.

claim: The severity of Hematodinium sp. colonisation of tissues is not attributed to collateral infections.
source: Crucially, the severity of Hematodinium sp. colonisation of tissues – either solid or liquid – is not attributed to collateral infections either.
evidence: This is a conclusion from regression analyses testing parasite load as a predictor of co-infections.

claim: Co-infection occurrence is decoupled from Hematodinium sp., with location being the main determinant.
source: Therefore, we contest that co-infection occurrence is decoupled from Hematodinium sp., with location being the main determinant (habitat or surrounding diversity; Davies et al., 2019b, Davies et al., 2020c).
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the statistical analyses with supporting citations.

claim: No immune cell reactivity was observed in vitro or in vivo towards Hematodinium sp. in crabs in the absence and presence of other disease-causing agents or damaged tissue.
source: We did not observe immune cell reactivity in vitro or in vivo – phagocytosis, encapsulation, or melanisation – towards Hematodinium sp. in crabs in the absence and presence of other disease-causing agents or damaged tissue.
evidence: This summarizes the findings from microscopy, histology, and in vitro assays.

claim: If Hematodinium sp. was suppressing the immune system of crabs, more alternative opportunistic infections would be expected, but this is not observed.
source: If Hematodinium sp. was supressing the immune system of crabs, we would expect to see more alternative opportunistic infections (we do not) and/or a reduced capacity of the host to react to other agents (we do not).
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the absence of expected outcomes if immunosuppression occurred.

claim: If Hematodinium sp. was suppressing the immune system of crabs, a reduced capacity of the host to react to other agents would be expected, but this is not observed.
source: If Hematodinium sp. was supressing the immune system of crabs, we would expect to see more alternative opportunistic infections (we do not) and/or a reduced capacity of the host to react to other agents (we do not).
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the observation that immune responses to other pathogens remain intact.

claim: Haemocyte-driven responses remain intact in early Hematodinium infections, but never target Hematodinium.
source: Haemocyte-driven responses remain intact in early infections, but never target Hematodinium.
evidence: This is a conclusion from histological and microscopic observations.

claim: Hematodinium sp. is considered to be a candidate immune evader of shore crab cellular defences.
source: We consider Hematodinium sp. to be a candidate immune evader of shore crab cellular defences.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings showing lack of cellular immune response to Hematodinium.

claim: The possibility of a potential immune-suppression mechanism at the molecular level by Hematodinium is not ruled out.
source: This does not rule out a potential immune-suppression mechanism at the molecular level.
evidence: This acknowledges limitations of the study which focused on cellular immunity.

claim: Several articles postulate that Hematodinium spp. suppression of the immune response is the most likely explanation for developing co-occurring secondary/opportunistic infections.
source: Several articles, including the expansive review by Stentiford and Shields, 2005, postulate that Hematodinium spp. suppression of the immune response of their crustacean hosts is the most likely explanation for developing co-occurring secondary/opportunistic infections, including septicaemia and ciliate infections in tanner crabs (C. bairdi; Love et al., 1993; Meyers et al., 1987) and yeast-like infections in edible crabs (C. pagurus), velvet swimming crabs (N. puber), and shore crabs (C. maenas; Smith et al., 2013; Stentiford et al., 2003).
evidence: This summarizes the prevailing hypothesis in the literature with citations.

claim: Crabs are compromised to a certain extent by the presence of Hematodinium spp., with host tissues and resources being replaced by accumulating dinoflagellate burden.
source: Crabs are compromised to a certain extent by the presence of Hematodinium spp., and as the infection progresses, the host's tissues and resources are replaced with the accumulating dinoflagellate burden, yet there is no mechanistic evidence to suggest that the parasite is directly suppressing the immune system.
evidence: This describes the pathological effects of infection while noting the lack of evidence for direct immunosuppression.

claim: There is no mechanistic evidence to suggest that Hematodinium parasites are directly suppressing the immune system.
source: Crabs are compromised to a certain extent by the presence of Hematodinium spp., and as the infection progresses, the host's tissues and resources are replaced with the accumulating dinoflagellate burden, yet there is no mechanistic evidence to suggest that the parasite is directly suppressing the immune system.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of the evidence for immunosuppression.

claim: Animals can be weakened in the absence of immunosuppression.
source: Animals can be weakened in the absence of immunosuppression.
evidence: This is a general biological principle relevant to interpreting the findings.

claim: Li et al., 2019 describe differential protein expression in the hepatopancreas of the gazami crab P. trituberculatus when parasitised by H. perezi in laboratory settings, including downregulation of factors associated with broad-spectrum pathogen recognition.
source: Li et al., 2019 describe differential protein expression in the hepatopancreas of the gazami crab P. trituberculatus when parasitised by H. perezi in laboratory settings, including the 'downregulation' of factors associated with broad-spectrum pathogen recognition.
evidence: This summarizes findings from a cited study.

claim: Based on the data, it is possible that Hematodinium sp. is an immune evader in shore crabs as its presence did not provoke cellular immunity or increase the likelihood of other diseases becoming established.
source: Based on these data, it is possible that Hematodinium sp. is an immune evader in shore crabs as its presence did not provoke cellular immunity or increase the likelihood of other diseases becoming established.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the collective findings.

claim: Stentiford et al., 2003 and Stentiford and Shields, 2005 note that there was surprisingly little evidence of host reactivity towards Hematodinium in crabs co-infected with yeast-like microbes.
source: Stentiford et al., 2003 and Stentiford and Shields, 2005 do note that there was surprisingly little evidence of host reactivity towards Hematodinium in crabs co-infected with yeast-like microbes.
evidence: This cites observations from previous studies supporting the immune evasion hypothesis.

claim: Mycosis is a rare event in the shore crabs studied (<0.3%).
source: Mycosis is a rare event in the shore crabs studied here (<0.3%; Davies et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the study with citation.

claim: Two crabs were harbouring both yeast-like and Hematodinium sp. microbes, but haemocyte-derived nodulation and phagocytosis were restricted to the fungus alone.
source: Two crabs were harbouring both yeast-like and Hematodinium sp. microbes, but haemocyte-derived nodulation and phagocytosis were restricted to the fungus alone.
evidence: This is an observation from histological examination of co-infected crabs.

claim: Phagocytosis and encapsulation/nodule formation are the main cellular immune responses in invertebrates.
source: Phagocytosis and encapsulation/nodule formation (a process where haemocytes wall off would-be colonisers) are the main cellular immune responses in invertebrates (Ratcliffe et al., 1985; Coates et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge about invertebrate immunity with citations.

claim: Direct observation of live haemocytes revealed that even in cases where there are large numbers of free Hematodinium in circulation, the haemocytes failed to recognise these as foreign.
source: Direct observation of live haemocytes revealed that even in cases where there are large numbers of free Hematodinium in circulation the haemocytes failed to recognise these as foreign.
evidence: This is an observation from live cell microscopy experiments.

claim: Nodules and capsules seen histologically in the tissues of Hematodinium-positive crabs did not contain Hematodinium parasites.
source: Similarly, nodules and capsules seen histologically in the tissues of Hematodinium-positive crabs did not contain such parasites, suggesting an active mechanism to avoid accidental incorporation into these defensive structures, perhaps molecular mimicry or concealment of surface ligands in a similar manner to entomopathogenic fungi in insect systems (reviewed by Butt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an observation from histological examination.

claim: The absence of Hematodinium in immune nodules suggests an active mechanism to avoid accidental incorporation into defensive structures, perhaps molecular mimicry or concealment of surface ligands.
source: Similarly, nodules and capsules seen histologically in the tissues of Hematodinium-positive crabs did not contain such parasites, suggesting an active mechanism to avoid accidental incorporation into these defensive structures, perhaps molecular mimicry or concealment of surface ligands in a similar manner to entomopathogenic fungi in insect systems (reviewed by Butt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the histological observations with citation to analogous systems.

claim: Preliminary laboratory studies revealed that C. pagurus with modest Hematodinium infections cleared bacteria with similar dynamics to those free from such infections.
source: Preliminary laboratory-based studies have revealed that C. pagurus with modest Hematodinium infections cleared bacteria with similar dynamics to those free from such infections (Smith and Rowley, 2015), implying that alleged immune suppression by Hematodinium has no effect on susceptibility to unrelated infections at least in early-mid phase.
evidence: This cites findings from a previous experimental study.

claim: Alleged immune suppression by Hematodinium has no effect on susceptibility to unrelated infections at least in early-mid phase of infection.
source: Preliminary laboratory-based studies have revealed that C. pagurus with modest Hematodinium infections cleared bacteria with similar dynamics to those free from such infections (Smith and Rowley, 2015), implying that alleged immune suppression by Hematodinium has no effect on susceptibility to unrelated infections at least in early-mid phase.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from cited experimental results.

claim: Late infections by Hematodinium cause a marked reduction in defensive cells in circulation.
source: Late infections by Hematodinium cause a marked reduction in defensive cells in circulation (Smith and Rowley, 2015), and these authors ascribed this to a side effect of metabolic exhaustion rather than targeted inhibition of haematopoiesis.
evidence: This cites an observation from a previous study.

claim: The reduction in defensive cells during late Hematodinium infection is ascribed to a side effect of metabolic exhaustion rather than targeted inhibition of haematopoiesis.
source: Late infections by Hematodinium cause a marked reduction in defensive cells in circulation (Smith and Rowley, 2015), and these authors ascribed this to a side effect of metabolic exhaustion rather than targeted inhibition of haematopoiesis.
evidence: This cites an interpretation from a previous study.

claim: Li et al., 2015a, 2015b presented evidence for parasite detection (immune recognition) and immune suppression in P. trituberculatus containing Hematodinium sp., based on measurements of candidate immune gene expression (mRNAs) and some enzymatic activities linked to defence.
source: Conversely, Li et al., 2015a; Li et al., 2015b presented evidence for parasite detection (immune recognition) and immune suppression in the P. trituberculatus containing Hematodinium sp., based on measurements of candidate immune gene expression (mRNAs) and some enzymatic activities linked to defence (e.g., phenoloxidase).
evidence: This summarizes findings from cited studies.

claim: In studies by Li et al., the selected immune genes were not expressed/suppressed consistently across the 8-day experimental period.
source: Regarding these studies, it is noteworthy that the selected immune genes were not expressed/suppressed consistently across the 8-day experimental period, there was a lack of correlation between haemograms and enzymic activities (no distinction between active and total phenoloxidase activities), protein levels were not quantitated so it is unclear if increased mRNAs led to more protein, and the mode of crab inoculation itself is likely to induce at least a localised inflammatory response.
evidence: This is a critical evaluation of the methodology and findings of cited studies.

claim: Li et al. suggested that P. trituberculatus recognise the presence of Hematodinium sp. and employ oxidising/nitrosative radicals (O2- and NO) and miRNAs to thwart the parasite.
source: Subsequently, the authors suggested that P. trituberculatus recognise the presence of Hematodinium sp. and employ oxidising/nitrosative radicals (O2- and NO) and miRNAs to thwart the parasite (Li et al., 2018; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This summarizes hypotheses from cited studies.

claim: The possibility that humoral (soluble)-mediated defences are involved in anti-Hematodinium immunity cannot be ruled out.
source: From our data, we cannot rule out the possibility that humoral (soluble)-mediated defences are involved in anti-Hematodinium immunity.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the study which focused on cellular immunity.

claim: The presence of one or more collateral infections overall (regardless of Hematodinium sp. presence) was characterised by the size of the animal.
source: Our study showed that the presence of one or more collateral infections overall (regardless of Hematodinium sp. presence or not) was characterised by the size of the animal.
evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis.

claim: The fact that autotomised crabs (those with missing limbs) are less likely to develop co-infections suggests the damage/trauma may temporarily 'prime' the immune system.
source: The fact that autotomised crabs (i.e., those with missing limbs) are less likely to develop co-infections is intriguing – suggesting the damage/trauma may temporarily 'prime' the immune system.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the finding about limb loss.

claim: There is some evidence that autotomy and ablation initiate stress responses in the crab Eriocheir sinensis, linked to differential haemocyte counts.
source: There is some evidence that autotomy and ablation initiate stress responses in another crab, Eriocheir sinensis, linked to differential haemocyte counts (Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: This cites evidence from another species supporting the immune priming hypothesis.

claim: Juvenile crustaceans are known to be at higher risk of contracting disease when compared to their older counterparts.
source: This is to be expected as juvenile crustaceans are known to be at higher risk of contracting disease when compared to their older counterparts (Ashby and Bruns, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about disease susceptibility with citation.

claim: Larger crustaceans have longer moult increments (therefore moult less often) than smaller, younger individuals.
source: Larger crustaceans have longer moult increments (therefore moult less often) than smaller, younger individuals (Castro and Angell, 2000), giving more time for co-infections to manifest.
evidence: This is established knowledge about crustacean biology with citation.

claim: It is postulated that Hematodinium zoospores use the soft cuticle found in newly moulted crabs as a portal of entry to the haemocoel.
source: Indeed, it is postulated that Hematodinium zoospores use the soft cuticle found in newly moulted crabs as a portal of entry to the haemocoel.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the infection route of Hematodinium.

claim: Injury or breaching of the cuticle can act as a portal of entry for microparasites.
source: Injury or breaching of the cuticle can act as a portal of entry for microparasites (Davies et al., 2015; Coates et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge about infection routes with citations.

claim: Co-infection incidence or composition did not follow established seasonal patterns associated with Hematodinium dynamics in shore crabs.
source: Co-infection incidence or composition did not follow established seasonal patterns associated with Hematodinium dynamics in this host (Supplementary file 2—table 1) – high severity and low prevalence in the winter, followed by low severity and high prevalence in the spring (Davies et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is a finding from temporal analysis with citation to previous work on Hematodinium seasonality.

claim: No temporal patterns of collateral infection cases were found in either Hematodinium-positive or Hematodinium-free animals.
source: No temporal patterns of collateral infection cases were found in either Hematodinium-positive or Hematodinium-free animals.
evidence: This is a finding from temporal analysis of co-infection data.

claim: No evidence of genetic differentiation was found between crabs sampled from the Dock and Pier, with both locations exhibiting similar genetic heterogeneity.
source: In addition, we found no evidence of genetic differentiation between crabs – and their resident Hematodinium ecotypes – sampled from the Dock and Pier, with both locations exhibiting similar genetic heterogeneity (Figure 1, Appendix 1—Tables 1–3, Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion from population genetic analyses shown in Figure 1 and appendix tables.

claim: The lack of substantive genetic diversity of host and Hematodinium between the sites is unlikely to account for the different disease profiles recorded.
source: The lack of substantive genetic diversity of host and Hematodinium between the sites is unlikely to account for the different disease profiles recorded, as such; the evidence implies that disease contraction in shore crabs depends on their environment.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the genetic and disease data.

claim: The evidence implies that disease contraction in shore crabs depends on their environment.
source: The lack of substantive genetic diversity of host and Hematodinium between the sites is unlikely to account for the different disease profiles recorded, as such; the evidence implies that disease contraction in shore crabs depends on their environment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined genetic and disease data.

claim: Environmental conditions of the sites tend to differ, most likely due to the hydrology of a semi-enclosed Dock vs. an open-water Pier.
source: Environmental conditions of the sites tend to differ – most likely due to the hydrology of a semi-enclosed Dock vs. an open-water Pier.
evidence: This is an observation about the physical characteristics of the study sites.

claim: Changes in environmental factors such as pH, nitrogenous wastes, and xenobiotics can influence both host and pathogen, and the incidence of disease.
source: Changes in such environmental factors, as well as pH, nitrogenous wastes, and xenobiotics, can influence both host and pathogen, and the incidence of disease (reviewed by Coates and Söderhäll, 2021).
